review_text_clean: Extremely disappointing and disrespectful experience. I will not be returning ever again. They scam you if you're paying with $50 bills or $100 in cash. From the moment my friends and I arrived, the male bartender with locs and a mustache serving us had an unnecessary attitude toward me. We understood that the bar was busy, so we initially gave him the benefit of the doubt and assumed he might simply be having a bad day. I ordered a $17 drink and a $12 appetizer and paid with a $50 bill. He gave me only 44 cents and did not give me a receipt. I was confused because the change was clearly incorrect, so when he saw my visible confusion he asked, "What's wrong?" I calmly and politely told him, "The change is incorrect. I gave you a $50 bill." Instead of explaining the transaction or correcting the change, he simply printed a receipt, slapped it down on the bar, and walked away. The receipt showed that I had supposedly given him $32, even though I had given him $50. Based on the total, he should have given me significantly more change. I was not rude, confrontational, or belligerent. I simply pointed out that the amount was wrong. I chose not to argue because I was not going to let the situation ruin my night and he was clearly not going to correct his error. Unfortunately, his behavior only became worse. My appetizer took well over 15-20 minutes to arrive. Since my group of friends and I were ready to leave, I politely asked for the appetizer could be cancelled because it still had not arrived and to get a refund. He immediately shook his head and said, "No, it's already being made," and slightly chuckled in an extremely dismissive manner. I understand that an order may already be in preparation, but he could have been professional. His response left my girl friend shocked as well. What was especially disturbing was that his disrespect toward me noticeably escalated after my guy friend left to step outside . My girlfriend even asked whether something was wrong because she noticed the change in his demeanor. We had been patient and understanding because the bar was busy, yet he continued treating me as though I had personally offended him, even though I had done nothing to him. Yet other customers weren't receiving this treatment we were getting from him. The girl working directly beside him witnessed the interaction and never checked in. While we were dealing with the situation, a server eventually brought the appetizer. I apologized to him and asked him to give it to someone else and let them know it was on the house because I no longer wanted it and did not want the situation to escalate further. When my male friend returned inside to understand what had happened, the bartender's demeanor suddenly changed. He was much more pleasant toward my friend and even gave him an inaccurate version of events, including claiming that he had offered to package the food for me to take home. That was never offered to me. Two of our other friends witnessed the interaction and noticed the clear difference in how he treated me compared with how he treated my male friend. I have worked in hospitality management for over 15 years, so I understand busy restaurants, kitchen delays, difficult customers, and orders that may already be in preparation. None of that excuses dismissive or hostile customer service. This was not about the $12 appetizer. It was not even about the incorrect change from the $50 bill. It was about being treated with unnecessary disrespect after calmly pointing out that I had not received the correct change, then being dismissed when I asked to cancel an appetizer that had not arrived, followed by an obvious change in demeanor once a guy customer became involved. I left feeling disrespected, dismissed, and singled out. I came in intending to enjoy myself and spend money at the establishment. Instead, I had to repeatedly defend why I deserved basic courtesy. There are too many places in NYC where I can spend my money and receive professional, respectful service. I will not be returning to Pretty Ricky's.

review_text_clean: I went in today wanting to order a plain black decaf coffee. The employee helping me initially was having a hard time explaining that they didn't offer decaf drip coffee, so I was already a little confused. Another employee working at the register next to him, who was Black, overheard the conversation and stepped in to explain that they only had decaf espresso. I don't know a lot about coffee and had never ordered plain espresso before, so I genuinely didn't understand the difference or what my options were. Instead of simply explaining it, the employee became noticeably loud and condescending toward me. I even apologized for not knowing the difference and asked what he would recommend since I didn't want a drink with milk. He asked whether I drank much coffee, and when I said not very often, he told me to get tea because I probably wouldn't like the espresso. I had specifically come in wanting coffee, so I decided to try the decaf espresso. His attitude throughout the interaction made me feel judged and uncomfortable for simply asking questions about something I wasn't familiar with. What bothered me most was that as I was leaving, I could hear that same employee talking to his coworkers about me ordering the espresso and making snarky comments about it. At that point, it went beyond an awkward interaction and felt unnecessarily disrespectful. I completely understand that a coffee shop may not carry the exact drink I was looking for, and I had no issue with that. I also understand that I wasn't familiar with the difference between decaf drip coffee and decaf espresso. But that shouldn't result in a customer being spoken down to or mocked afterward, especially when part of an employee's job is helping customers understand the menu and decide what to order. The espresso itself was disappointing, and the interaction made the entire experience even worse. I left feeling stupid and talked down to rather than helped.

review_text_clean: Last rainy Saturday, we had a lovely surprise at this restaurant. As someone who grew up in China, I honestly don't have very high expectations for Chinese restaurants in NYC. They almost always feel commercial to me-but not necessarily "commercially" good, even when they have excellent reviews. We were strolling around SoHo and chose this place for dinner almost randomly. Even before walking in, I saw two large groups of non-Chinese diners waiting by the entrance and thought to myself, another place that's probably just going to be OK. I couldn't have been more wrong. Except for the fact that the staff members we encountered spoke fluent English, everything else somehow felt so... Chinese. The service was friendly in exactly the right amount. No one kept coming over to ask, as a formality, whether "everything was good." At one point, I switched one dish for another, half "admitting" that I wanted to learn some tricks from that particular dish, and the waitress simply gave me this genuine, understanding smile. Later, all of our dishes had arrived except one, and we weren't quite sure whether it had actually been included in our order. When we asked another waitress, she immediately understood what we meant and responded in such a calm, reassuring way-without treating the question as if we were pushing her to hurry up with the dish. There's a nuanced difference there, if you know what I mean. The food also came out unexpectedly fast, and the flavors were spot-on. That, of course, is the biggest reason I came away thinking: this place is authentic. And then there was the space itself. When we were first seated, I felt lucky that the two of us had been given a four-person table. But once I sat down and looked around, I realized they simply weren't "stingy" with their seating arrangements. That kind of generosity with space is not particularly common in NYC restaurants. At first, I also thought the room was a little noisy and perhaps not very conducive to a deep conversation. Half an hour later, though, we found ourselves talking about our feelings toward different family members. Somehow, the ambience was just right: enough life and noise around us that you could let some emotion out, without the room becoming so quiet that you suddenly felt exposed and responsible for filling every silence. When we walked out, I said to myself, I really need to leave a positive review for this team. So I took one last picture before we left.

review_text_raw:
Last rainy Saturday, we had a lovely surprise at this restaurant.

As someone who grew up in China, I honestly don’t have very high expectations for Chinese restaurants in NYC. They almost always feel commercial to me—but not necessarily “commercially” good, even when they have excellent reviews.

We were strolling around SoHo and chose this place for dinner almost randomly. Even before walking in, I saw two large groups of non-Chinese diners waiting by the entrance and thought to myself, another place that’s probably just going to be OK.

I couldn’t have been more wrong.

Except for the fact that the staff members we encountered spoke fluent English, everything else somehow felt so… Chinese.

The service was friendly in exactly the right amount. No one kept coming over to ask, as a formality, whether “everything was good.” At one point, I switched one dish for another, half “admitting” that I wanted to learn some tricks from that particular dish, and the waitress simply gave me this genuine, understanding smile.

Later, all of our dishes had arrived except one, and we weren’t quite sure whether it had actually been included in our order. When we asked another waitress, she immediately understood what we meant and responded in such a calm, reassuring way—without treating the question as if we were pushing her to hurry up with the dish.

There’s a nuanced difference there, if you know what I mean.

The food also came out unexpectedly fast, and the flavors were spot-on. That, of course, is the biggest reason I came away thinking: this place is authentic.

And then there was the space itself.

When we were first seated, I felt lucky that the two of us had been given a four-person table. But once I sat down and looked around, I realized they simply weren’t “stingy” with their seating arrangements. That kind of generosity with space is not particularly common in NYC restaurants.

At first, I also thought the room was a little noisy and perhaps not very conducive to a deep conversation. Half an hour later, though, we found ourselves talking about our feelings toward different family members. Somehow, the ambience was just right: enough life and noise around us that you could let some emotion out, without the room becoming so quiet that you suddenly felt exposed and responsible for filling every silence.

When we walked out, I said to myself, I really need to leave a positive review for this team.

So I took one last picture before we left.

review_text_clean: Friends were visiting and wanted to go for Happy Hour to Madam Ji Ki Shadi. Translates to "Madam's wedding." As I stepped into this restaurant the first painting on the left I saw was that of a mujra - courtesan. Naturally, Mussafar Ali's epic Umrao Jaan came to mind. In some Indian weddings, a mujra dances for entertainment. The interior is so pretty that one feels happy being here. Shobha and Sumi were already here and having a Madamji Martini and a vodka tonic. The happy hour menu is short but varied. An order of three plump vegetable samosas at $7 each was expensive. The flavor was average. Crispy Okra and Masala Fries were far tastier. All three came with their own sauces in tiny ramekins. Who doesn't like crispy okra? Shobha is very fond of them as am I and Sumi likes fries a lot. Here they were both salty and peppery. In short- finger licking tasty! Mango lassi decorated with rose petals was my chosen drink and it was creamy and thankfully not too sweet. We enjoyed the food and later said hello to the chef. I plan on returning. Highly recommended.

When we asked how we were supposed to eat them, we were told that they were meant to be used almost like a spoon for the mayonnaise. Toward the end, we also got the impression that they wanted us to pay and leave as soon as possible, even though the restaurant was fairly empty. Overall, despite the lovely atmosphere, good wine, and tasty main dishes, the experience was unfortunately overshadowed by the service and the appetizer, and we left without much desire to come back.

review_text_clean: The atmosphere here is immaculate, but unfortunately, the service left a lot to be desired. My friends and I stopped in on Saturday night, and the place was still lively and packed. After asking our waitress for recommendations, we decided to order a more affordable bottle of pinot. We were surprised when the more expensive gruner was brought to our table instead - and it was served completely warm. When we tried to clarify the mix-up with our waitress, we felt ignored. The wine was so warm that we repeatedly had to ask for ice just to make it drinkable. To make matters even stranger, another waiter told us that he wanted to go home and asked if he could give us to-go cups so we could leave, without really offering another option. I genuinely love the vibe and atmosphere of this place, but if the staff didn't have the time or capacity to accommodate a full bottle service that night, it would have been better to be upfront about that. The restaurant was busy both indoors and outdoors, but that shouldn't come at the expense of the guest experience. Honesty and good communication go a long way. If you're going to serve a bottle of wine, especially at a busy venue, please make sure it's properly chilled - or served with an ice bucket. I'd love to see the service match the atmosphere, because the potential is definitely there.

review_text_clean: The Melancholy of the Reheated: Pomme Frites Loses its Mojo There is an alchemy to the humble frites of Belgium, a crisp, golden outer shell yielding to a pillowy, steaming interior, forged through the sacred ritual of the double-fry. For years, the East Village sanctuary known as Pomme Frites was New York's improbable temple to this art. To walk into the original postage-stamp storefront on Second Avenue was to inhale a heady, unapologetic cloud of beef tallow and anticipation. They were freshly cut, meticulously crafted, and utterly transcendent. The resurrection of Pomme Frites in the neighborhood should have been a culinary triumph. Instead, it is a sobering exercise in nostalgia unfulfilled. The fries arriving at the table today bear no resemblance to their exalted predecessor. Gone is the earthy, irregular charm of the freshly butchered potato. In their place are glorifed diner fries- uniform, industrialized, and unmistakably frozen. They possess the hollow, cardboard crunch of mass production, lacking both structural integrity and soul. They are the sort of side dish one apathetically pushes to the side of a mediocre bistro plate, a ghost of a recipe processed for convenience rather than reverence. The kitchen's distraction appears entirely diverted toward camouflage. The venue leans heavily on an overkill of gimmicky sauces-dozens of flavoredmayos and artisanal drizzles that arrive like a colorful defense mechanism. It is a cynical sleight of hand: if you bury a mediocre starch under truffle-garlic aioli and mango chutney, does anyone notice the tragedy beneath? If even a fraction of the energy expended on curating an endless wall of condiments had been invested in the actual potato; in sourcing, cutting, and executing a proper made-to-order fry, there might have been a product worth cheering for. As it stands, the soul has unceremoniously departed the premises, leaving behind only a branded shell. Two stars, awarded purely out of respect for the sheer effort of keeping the lights on.

There is an alchemy to the humble frites of Belgium, a crisp, golden outer shell yielding to a pillowy, steaming interior, forged through the sacred ritual of the double-fry. For years, the East Village sanctuary known as Pomme Frites was New York’s improbable temple to this art. To walk into the original postage-stamp storefront on Second Avenue was to inhale a heady, unapologetic cloud of beef tallow and anticipation. They were freshly cut, meticulously crafted, and utterly transcendent.
The resurrection of Pomme Frites in the neighborhood should have been a culinary triumph. Instead, it is a sobering exercise in nostalgia unfulfilled.
The fries arriving at the table today bear no resemblance to their exalted predecessor. Gone is the earthy, irregular charm of the freshly butchered potato. In their place are glorifed diner fries- uniform, industrialized, and unmistakably frozen. They possess the hollow, cardboard crunch of mass production, lacking both structural integrity and soul. They are the sort of side dish one apathetically pushes to the side of a mediocre bistro plate, a ghost of a recipe processed for convenience rather than reverence.
The kitchen’s distraction appears entirely diverted toward camouflage. The venue leans heavily on an overkill of gimmicky sauces—dozens of flavoredmayos and artisanal drizzles that arrive like a colorful defense mechanism. It is a cynical sleight of hand: if you bury a mediocre starch under truffle-garlic aioli and mango chutney, does anyone notice the tragedy beneath?
If even a fraction of the energy expended on curating an endless wall of condiments had been invested in the actual potato; in sourcing, cutting, and executing a proper made-to-order fry, there might have been a product worth cheering for. As it stands, the soul has unceremoniously departed the premises, leaving behind only a branded shell. Two stars, awarded purely out of respect for the sheer effort of keeping the lights on.

No tables will be available, as these are reservation only. Most recently, I dined with a table reservation last week. Reservations are difficult to snag. I was able to book through Resy after I set up alerts for cancellations. This is only really a reliable method if you have priority status on Resy by being an AMEX platinum card holder, because you will get the alerts first. Despite being 25 minutes late (nyc traffic), they allowed us to sit at our table. We had exceptional service and delicious food. Our server was extremely knowledgeable on our options as vegans. He was able to recommend a cucumber appetizer and two different pastas. The cucumbers were a huge surprise and stole the show. The pastas were also incredible. We were there celebrating our anniversary, and they sent us a beautiful display of fruit on ice in a large bowl and a sorbet dessert. I would dine at this place during every visit to the city. Highly, highly recommend for anybody and everybody.

To start, we enjoyed a perfectly prepared salmon tartare. For our main courses, we chose filet and sirloin steak. The meat was incredibly tender, superbly seasoned, and grilled to perfection - simply delicious! The various wines from different wine regions, which we sampled by the glass, were all excellent. Top marks for the outstanding food, the beautiful ambiance, and the attentive, warm service! We thoroughly enjoyed our evening and would love to return anytime.

review_text_clean: The service, music, ambiance, and food here are absolutely amazing! From the moment we walked in, the staff was incredibly friendly and attentive, making us feel welcome right away. Their cocktail game is top-tier, the drinks are perfectly balanced with a creative twist. We started with a dirty martini, a mezcal penicillin, and a glass of wine, all of which were excellent. For appetizers, we ordered the crispy tuna fries and the hamachi. Both were incredibly fresh, but what really stands out is how unique the sauces are. Everything is prepared to absolute perfection. For our main course, we split the duck adobo and the fried rice, and it did not disappoint. During dinner, Chef Josh actually came over to our table to talk to us. He shared the inspiration behind the menu, explaining his incredible fusion of French and Filipino culinary styles, and mentioned that his mentor worked with Jean-Georges for a long time. You can truly taste that world-class pedigree in every single bite. I highly recommend coming to this restaurant for an unforgettable meal. Plus, if you are looking to keep the night going, they transition into a club after 10 PM. We will definitely be back!

The tempura was perfectly light and crispy, and the oden was absolutely delicious, with the broth and flavor soaked into every bite. Paired with Japanese sake, it was just perfect. There was something very special about being able to enjoy the kind of delicious food I would eat in Japan, right here in New York. As someone from Japan, it genuinely made me happy and brought back memories of home. Yopparai isn't just a place to eat Japanese food - it's a place where you can experience the warmth and comfort of a real Japanese izakaya. Great food, great sake, and a wonderful atmosphere. If you're looking for an authentic izakaya experience in New York, I highly recommend Yopparai.

review_text_clean: i've liked matchaful for years, especially their matcha soft serve, so this is coming from someone who genuinely wanted to keep liking the brand. i went to the soho location and got the 16 oz mango cold foam matcha for $11.43 after tax (it's one sized so the price being that is even more questioning hmm). the staff were excellent - i took a good 3-6 minutes deciding, asked questions, changed my mind a few times, and they stayed patient, gave recommendations, and never made me feel rushed. the space is also nice, especially the seating along the windows if you want to sit for a bit. the drink itself tasted good, but this is where i have a problem with the price. the mango was strong, creamy, and easily the dominant flavor. the matcha was so subtle that my immediate comparison was honestly mango lassi with matcha somewhere in the background. if this were an $8-ish fruit drink, i probably wouldn't think much of it. at $11.43 from a business built around matcha, i expected the tea itself to be one of the most noticeable parts of the drink. i actually looked into the recipe afterward because i didn't want to complain about the price just because "$11 sounds expensive." matchaful lists 4g of hikari matcha, mango purée, housemade oat milk, agave, and mango-coconut cold foam. their hikari is legitimately well-sourced japanese matcha, so i'm not accusing them of using cheap powder. there are real ingredients and extra prep here. but researching it also made me less convinced by the value, not more. other serious matcha shops are able to make the tea itself much more central at lower prices. kettl, one of the more established japanese tea specialists in nyc, also uses 4g in its own latte recipe and literally describes its approach as making the matcha the star. current listings put its iced ceremonial matcha latte around $7.50. 12 matcha is another very matcha-focused shop using first-harvest matcha, and recent customer reports put a latte around the same $7-8 range. obviously those are not identical drinks. matchaful is adding mango and a separate cold foam, so an upcharge makes sense. i'm not expecting a specialty fruit drink to cost exactly the same as a plain latte. i just don't think mango, oat milk and cold foam automatically bridge the gap to an almost $12 experience when the most expensive and supposedly distinctive ingredient was one of the least noticeable things i tasted. and to be fair, matchaful isn't uniquely doing this. there are other nyc specialty matcha shops charging around $10-11 before tax for elaborate fruit matchas with cold foam. so this is partly where the market is going. but "other places charge this much too" explains the price -> it doesn't automatically prove the value. that's really where i land on matchaful. i'm not upset that premium matcha costs money. i'll happily pay more when i can actually taste why i'm paying more. what bothered me here is that the premium sounded much clearer on the ingredient list than it tasted in the cup. the service was genuinely great, the atmosphere was nice, and i enjoyed drinking it. i'm not calling it a bad drink. i just think there's a meaningful difference between a drink being good and a drink being worth $11.43. overall: great service, nice atmosphere, thoughtful ingredients, enjoyable flavor, but weak matcha presence and poor value at this price. i'd still come back for the soft serve or try something more matcha-forward, but i would not order this particular drink again for or any other drink adding up to $11.43 😿.

i’ve liked matchaful for years, especially their matcha soft serve, so this is coming from someone who genuinely wanted to keep liking the brand. i went to the soho location and got the 16 oz mango cold foam matcha for $11.43 after tax (it’s one sized so the price being that is even more questioning hmm). the staff were excellent - i took a good 3–6 minutes deciding, asked questions, changed my mind a few times, and they stayed patient, gave recommendations, and never made me feel rushed. the space is also nice, especially the seating along the windows if you want to sit for a bit.

the drink itself tasted good, but this is where i have a problem with the price. the mango was strong, creamy, and easily the dominant flavor. the matcha was so subtle that my immediate comparison was honestly mango lassi with matcha somewhere in the background. if this were an $8-ish fruit drink, i probably wouldn’t think much of it. at $11.43 from a business built around matcha, i expected the tea itself to be one of the most noticeable parts of the drink.

i actually looked into the recipe afterward because i didn’t want to complain about the price just because “$11 sounds expensive.” matchaful lists 4g of hikari matcha, mango purée, housemade oat milk, agave, and mango-coconut cold foam. their hikari is legitimately well-sourced japanese matcha, so i’m not accusing them of using cheap powder. there are real ingredients and extra prep here.

but researching it also made me less convinced by the value, not more. other serious matcha shops are able to make the tea itself much more central at lower prices. kettl, one of the more established japanese tea specialists in nyc, also uses 4g in its own latte recipe and literally describes its approach as making the matcha the star. current listings put its iced ceremonial matcha latte around $7.50. 12 matcha is another very matcha-focused shop using first-harvest matcha, and recent customer reports put a latte around the same $7–8 range.

obviously those are not identical drinks. matchaful is adding mango and a separate cold foam, so an upcharge makes sense. i’m not expecting a specialty fruit drink to cost exactly the same as a plain latte. i just don’t think mango, oat milk and cold foam automatically bridge the gap to an almost $12 experience when the most expensive and supposedly distinctive ingredient was one of the least noticeable things i tasted.

and to be fair, matchaful isn’t uniquely doing this. there are other nyc specialty matcha shops charging around $10–11 before tax for elaborate fruit matchas with cold foam. so this is partly where the market is going. but “other places charge this much too” explains the price —> it doesn’t automatically prove the value.

that’s really where i land on matchaful. i’m not upset that premium matcha costs money. i’ll happily pay more when i can actually taste why i’m paying more. what bothered me here is that the premium sounded much clearer on the ingredient list than it tasted in the cup.

the service was genuinely great, the atmosphere was nice, and i enjoyed drinking it. i’m not calling it a bad drink. i just think there’s a meaningful difference between a drink being good and a drink being worth $11.43.

overall: great service, nice atmosphere, thoughtful ingredients, enjoyable flavor, but weak matcha presence and poor value at this price. i’d still come back for the soft serve or try something more matcha-forward, but i would not order this particular drink again for or any other drink adding up to $11.43 😿.

review_text_clean: The food at Corima is honestly wonderful: creative, surprising and, most importantly, really delicious. There were several dishes I absolutely loved, which is why I was a little sad that the overall experience didn't quite feel like five stars to me. The food itself is the clear highlight, and I would genuinely love to return, especially to try the à la carte menu. The tasting menu included some excellent and memorable dishes. However, I didn't realise when booking through Resy that the tasting menu was the only option attached to our reservation. We weren't shown a food menu or asked whether we preferred the tasting menu or à la carte. Later, I saw the couple next to us enjoying beautiful full-sized dishes and realised that à la carte was also available. Maybe I missed something while booking, but I really wish I had known, as their dinner looked like my dream meal. Personally, I would much rather have three amazing dishes and more than one bite of each than thirteen tiny courses. Unfortunately, the service and communication sometimes felt less polished than I had expected. When we arrived, there was nobody at the entrance, so we - along with another couple - walked into the restaurant before eventually coming back to find someone. I had also mentioned some food intolerances in my reservation and was told that the restaurant had tried several times to contact me by phone and email. I may have missed calls while travelling, but I never received an email. In the end, I explained that they were intolerances rather than allergies and that I could be flexible, so it wasn't really an issue, it was just the communication side that felt a little odd. There were also a few moments during the meal when clearer communication would have helped. We ordered the tortilla with caviar after seeing it at the table next to us. It arrived without caviar and without explanation. We asked again and ordered another one with caviar, but that one also arrived without it. Only when we asked a second time were we told that they had run out. Of course, restaurants run out of things, and that is absolutely no problem; I would simply have appreciated being told before the dish arrived twice. Something similar happened when we asked to add one of the à la carte dishes we had seen at the neighbouring table. We made clear that we didn't want to change the tasting menu, but simply wanted to add and pay for another dish. We were told that someone would check, but nobody came back to us. Once dessert arrived, we understood that it wasn't happening. None of these things individually is a major issue, and everyone on the team was genuinely lovely and kind. I think I simply expected the experience to feel a little more effortless and attentive at a Michelin-starred restaurant. The food absolutely deserves the praise, and I would happily come back to Corima, particularly to try the à la carte menu. I just wish the service and communication had been a little more refined and had made us feel slightly more looked after, because with food this good, that would have made the evening exceptional.

review_text_raw:
The food at Corima is honestly wonderful: creative, surprising and, most importantly, really delicious. There were several dishes I absolutely loved, which is why I was a little sad that the overall experience didn’t quite feel like five stars to me. The food itself is the clear highlight, and I would genuinely love to return, especially to try the à la carte menu.

The tasting menu included some excellent and memorable dishes. However, I didn’t realise when booking through Resy that the tasting menu was the only option attached to our reservation. We weren’t shown a food menu or asked whether we preferred the tasting menu or à la carte. Later, I saw the couple next to us enjoying beautiful full-sized dishes and realised that à la carte was also available. Maybe I missed something while booking, but I really wish I had known, as their dinner looked like my dream meal. Personally, I would much rather have three amazing dishes and more than one bite of each than thirteen tiny courses.

Unfortunately, the service and communication sometimes felt less polished than I had expected. When we arrived, there was nobody at the entrance, so we — along with another couple — walked into the restaurant before eventually coming back to find someone.

I had also mentioned some food intolerances in my reservation and was told that the restaurant had tried several times to contact me by phone and email. I may have missed calls while travelling, but I never received an email. In the end, I explained that they were intolerances rather than allergies and that I could be flexible, so it wasn’t really an issue, it was just the communication side that felt a little odd.

There were also a few moments during the meal when clearer communication would have helped. We ordered the tortilla with caviar after seeing it at the table next to us. It arrived without caviar and without explanation. We asked again and ordered another one with caviar, but that one also arrived without it. Only when we asked a second time were we told that they had run out. Of course, restaurants run out of things, and that is absolutely no problem; I would simply have appreciated being told before the dish arrived twice.

Something similar happened when we asked to add one of the à la carte dishes we had seen at the neighbouring table. We made clear that we didn’t want to change the tasting menu, but simply wanted to add and pay for another dish. We were told that someone would check, but nobody came back to us. Once dessert arrived, we understood that it wasn’t happening.

None of these things individually is a major issue, and everyone on the team was genuinely lovely and kind. I think I simply expected the experience to feel a little more effortless and attentive at a Michelin-starred restaurant. The food absolutely deserves the praise, and I would happily come back to Corima, particularly to try the à la carte menu. I just wish the service and communication had been a little more refined and had made us feel slightly more looked after, because with food this good, that would have made the evening exceptional.

review_text_clean: We arrived at Corima with a reservation, but no table was available, so we were seated at the bar. A few minutes later, the staff told us a table would open in about 15 minutes. We were eventually seated near the bar, rather than in the main dining room. We ordered two beers while at the bar, but they never reached us after we moved to a table just a few feet from the bartender. We ordered wine instead. From that point on, the service was excellent: attentive and cordial. The room was buzzing, but so noisy that conversation was difficult. The food, unfortunately, did not justify the excitement or the prices. The much-touted sourdough flour tortilla with recado negro butter was more like a gooey crepe, accompanied by butter I found tasteless. The cucumber, quelites, piparra, melon, and salsa macha dish was fresh and beautifully presented, though I couldn't detect the melon. It was good, but the description was more compelling than the dish. The wagyu beef and heart were well prepared and arranged in a handful of carefully cut pieces. There was very little to eat for the price. The turbot with epazote pil-pil and spring onions was the most interesting dish: it arrived with a hard skin enclosing flavorful, steaming fish. I would have liked more epazote, which seemed lost on the plate. Overall, Corima was a disappointment. Whatever the restaurant calls its cuisine, the meal bore little resemblance to the Mexican food I know and love. I can think of many restaurants where I would eat better, enjoy the atmosphere more, and spend less. I would not return simply because a place is trending; the food has to be the main event.

review_text_clean: I liked the room, which is annoying in retrospect. It was small, a little cramped, and full of the kind of references I grew up around in family restaurants. For a minute it felt quaint, familiar, like somebody's actual kitchen. The meal did not survive that impression. We had come for the fusion, that New York meeting of Hispanic and Chinese food, which is hardly a wild idea in this city. You would think someone in the building could talk about it. The waitress could not. Questions got hesitant, flummoxed half-answers, with no opinion and no sense of what was worth ordering. She set the plates down and left. Water was not refilled. A premade iced tea and a straw took about ten minutes. We were in the back booth by the bathroom, along one narrow walkway, so there was nowhere for her to pretend she was not passing us. She did, ten or twelve times, without a word, clearly clocking whether we were done. In a room that small, a stare is not subtle. The attention arrived for the exit and never for the meal. It felt scrutinized, and a little discriminatory. The portions were generous for the price, and that is the only credit I will give. The food was greasy, overcooked, and mushy, oversalted and still underseasoned, with a gamey edge that belonged to neither tradition. The broccoli beside the sesame chicken was the best thing on the table, which is a miserable thing to have to admit. Everything else tasted like a five-minute search for the dish it was supposed to be. A bastardization. The drinks were the same failure in a glass: too tart and sour, or so sweet the fruit had disappeared. I can speak for the Chinese side. The people with me can speak for the Hispanic side. None of us took this as gospel, and none of us were impressed. This city already has rooms that love both cuisines, and rooms that fuse them without embarrassing either one. This was the neighborhood worn as a costume. An overrated cash grab, with none of the love and none of the craft. I would not go back.

review_text_clean: I absolutely love Dudley's! I come here at least once a month, and it has easily become one of my favorite restaurants over the past 2-3 years. The food, service, and atmosphere are consistently great, and I've introduced so many friends to this place. That being said, I think being such a regular customer allows me to offer some honest feedback. On one occasion, I found a hair wrapped around my pancake after I had already covered it in syrup and was about to take my first bite. Of course, it was disappointing, but the staff handled it well, replaced my meal, and took it off the bill. Clearly, it didn't stop me from coming back! My biggest frustration is the inability to make reservations in the morning. I completely understand how busy brunch can get, especially on weekends and holidays, but I wish there were some flexibility. I tried making a reservation for Mother's Day because I wanted to bring my mom, but unfortunately, that wasn't an option. I also wanted to mention the menu changes following the renovations. The restaurant itself looks beautiful, and I appreciate the updates, but I genuinely miss the original steak frites. It used to be one of my favorite dishes on the menu! While I appreciate the addition of the smothered steak, the changes to the steak frites have been disappointing, and I've found myself coming in for dinner much less frequently because of it. Despite these few critiques, I really do love Dudley's. It's a place I consistently return to, recommend to others, and genuinely enjoy supporting. I was just here yesterday and I'm already coming back today! I hope this feedback is received in the spirit it's intended. I'm sharing it because I've been a loyal customer for years and would love to see a few of the things that originally made this place so special return. Dudley's is still one of my favorites, and I look forward to many more visits!

I came to the bar for a friend's birthday party, for which she had rented out the space. Domhnall was working the door and, while speaking to me, told me to look at him. I have strabismus, an eye condition that affects the alignment of my eyes, so looking directly at someone in the way he was demanding is not always something I can control. I calmly explained this to him. Instead of showing even a basic level of understanding, Donald accused me of having an "attitude" and told me I could not come inside. I had not been disrespectful or confrontational with him. I was simply trying to explain a physical condition that is completely outside of my control. What made the experience even more upsetting was that I was there to celebrate a friend's birthday at an event she had specifically rented the bar for, and I ultimately had to apologize to Donald (despite having done nothing wrong) just so that I would be allowed inside. No customer should be humiliated or denied entry because a physical condition is misinterpreted. As a woman, and particularly as someone with a condition that affects the way I make eye contact, being spoken to and treated this way by the owner of an establishment was incredibly upsetting. I left the interaction feeling singled out, embarrassed, and unwelcome over something I cannot control. I hope Domhnall takes some time to reflect on how he treats customers, particularly people with disabilities or physical differences that may affect the way they communicate or interact. No one should have to disclose a medical condition at the door of a bar and then apologize for it in order to be treated with basic dignity. Based on my experience, I cannot recommend supporting an establishment whose owner treats a customer this way, particularly after being explicitly told that the behavior he was criticizing was the result of a physical condition. review_text_clean: Went to Bonnie Vee for Game 5 of the Knicks (or so I thought). We had been there for about an hour and had just ordered a fresh round of drinks when, right as the game started, the manager announced that everyone needed to leave because there was a private party at 9 PM. At no point before entering were we told this information. In fact, we continued to be served drinks without any mention that we would be kicked out shortly after. It honestly felt misleading, as we came specifically to watch the game and expected to be able to stay. Understandably, the entire bar was upset and asking questions after the announcement. The woman with brown hair, who I assume was the manager, was incredibly unapologetic. She grabbed the remote, turned off the Knicks game, and told everyone to leave. The way the situation was handled felt unnecessarily rude and dismissive. This would have been a completely different situation if the bar had simply disclosed upfront that there was a private event and that patrons would need to leave before or during the game. To kick people out in the middle of the Knicks finals and force them to scramble to find another bar, without any prior warning, is awful customer service. What makes this even more frustrating is that Bonnie Vee had posted on Instagram that the Knicks game would be on at the bar. Had we known we wouldn't actually be able to watch it there, we never would have come in the first place. It's a shame because I was having a great time before this happened. Unfortunately, the lack of transparency and the way customers were treated completely ruined the experience. 1 star.

review_text_clean: Such a charming little place. I am a huge fan of beef patties, and over the years I have had to keep looking for new ones as the old ones change hands or move. So discovering this little place was a true find. I arrived on a Friday afternoon and purchased a bunch of beef patties for myself and a few for a friend of mine (she, too, is addicted). Unfortunately, I was too late for the sweet pies, as they had already sold out. If you are used to the classic turmeric-colored, flaky-crust patties, these are not that. This is a more refined patty. The dough is soft yet flavorful, and these patties are slightly smaller than I am used to but still larger than an empanada. Where these really sing is in the filling. Delicious beef and a true sense of the Scotch bonnet peppers, with a bit of heat but not off-putting at all. Just a perfect balance. As a NYC native and decade-long BKLYN resident, I have tried many patties in my day, and these stand up to anything along Eastern Parkway in their own original way. Five Stars!!!!

The spicy tuna was drowning in spicy mayo, the salmon was covered in an unappetizing green sauce, and the scallop (usually my favorite) had an overpowering truffle-like flavor that completely ruined it. For a restaurant specializing in hand rolls, I expected much better. Places like KazuNori and Sushi Takoro do an excellent job of letting the freshness and quality of the fish speak for itself, rather than masking it with heavy sauces and competing flavors. Great vibe, but the food needs serious work. I really wanted to like this place, but I left disappointed.

review_text_clean: We went to Raf's on the recommendation of a friend who lives in New York, and it was definitely a great choice for breakfast/brunch. The place has that very New York style, but at the same time, you can tell they're quite good at everything related to bread, pastries, and puff pastries. There were five of us, so we took the opportunity to order quite a few things to share: - Soft scrambled eggs with toast and spinach: very good. The eggs were perfectly cooked, and the toast was also especially good. - Seasonal fruit bowl: beautifully presented, with a good variety of fruit and a fairly generous portion. - Omelette: one of their most popular dishes and highly recommended. Very well executed. - Tartine: also very good. It's a slightly more substantial option, but well worth it. - Yogurt bowl: with fruit, granola, and nuts. Another very complete option that we quite enjoyed. Perhaps the least impressive aspect was the coffee. The food is quite basic and lacks attention to detail compared to the quality of the food. It's that typical American diner coffee shop where this aspect feels somewhat neglected. The service was rather slow, and we had to wait quite a while for our food, which surprised us, especially since the restaurant was practically empty at the time. However, they made a nice gesture to compensate: they gave us a free ham and cheese croissant, which was delicious, and also a cookie that we took with us for later. As for the price, it's not cheap. We paid around $200 for five people, which is a considerable amount for breakfast, although it's also true that we ordered a lot and didn't skimp too much. Overall, a good experience, especially because of the quality of the food, the bread, and the pastries. The service could be a bit faster, and the coffee could be better prepared, especially considering the price point, but even so, I think it's a recommendable place for breakfast or brunch in New York.

We went to Raf’s on the recommendation of a friend who lives in New York, and it was definitely a great choice for breakfast/brunch. The place has that very New York style, but at the same time, you can tell they're quite good at everything related to bread, pastries, and puff pastries.

There were five of us, so we took the opportunity to order quite a few things to share:

- Soft scrambled eggs with toast and spinach: very good. The eggs were perfectly cooked, and the toast was also especially good.

- Seasonal fruit bowl: beautifully presented, with a good variety of fruit and a fairly generous portion.

- Omelette: one of their most popular dishes and highly recommended. Very well executed.

- Tartine: also very good. It's a slightly more substantial option, but well worth it.

- Yogurt bowl: with fruit, granola, and nuts. Another very complete option that we quite enjoyed.

Perhaps the least impressive aspect was the coffee. The food is quite basic and lacks attention to detail compared to the quality of the food. It's that typical American diner coffee shop where this aspect feels somewhat neglected.

The service was rather slow, and we had to wait quite a while for our food, which surprised us, especially since the restaurant was practically empty at the time. However, they made a nice gesture to compensate: they gave us a free ham and cheese croissant, which was delicious, and also a cookie that we took with us for later.

As for the price, it's not cheap. We paid around $200 for five people, which is a considerable amount for breakfast, although it's also true that we ordered a lot and didn't skimp too much.

Overall, a good experience, especially because of the quality of the food, the bread, and the pastries. The service could be a bit faster, and the coffee could be better prepared, especially considering the price point, but even so, I think it's a recommendable place for breakfast or brunch in New York.

review_text_clean: As someone who does not normally write reviews, I'd like to advise others to BE CAREFUL. They are very inconsistent with their prices. Sometimes they charge about $8 per dish, just recently I was charged $10. There were also two occasions I was given a completely different dish than ordered and the woman at the front gave me a difficult time for trying to open the containers to check before leaving. On another occasion, I gave more cash than was owed (a few extra dollar bills) and the same woman at the front claimed I never gave it in the first place. I don't normally write reviews, but be very careful when ordering since the woman can be very dishonest. They only take cash and do not give receipts so if I were to go back, I'd at least record myself ordering and ask for the price upfront. As someone Chinese who orders in Mandarin Chinese, I also suspect that they are biased towards Fuzhounese speaking customers. On a positive note, the food is great and fulfilling. There are many unique Fuzhounese dishes that I cannot Find elsewhere in the city. I'm not someone who writes reviews often. However, I want to share my experience at this restaurant, hoping to warn others. Their food prices are inconsistent; sometimes they charge me $8, sometimes $10, even though the menu shows $8 for a plate of rice. Recently, I was charged $10. I ordered sweet and sour fish fillets, but they charged me $10, when it's usually $8. And when I got home and opened the order, I discovered they had given me the wrong order. Also, when I picked up the delivery before, I tried to open it to check if it was the correct order, and the woman at the counter was whispering and giving me unfriendly looks. So this time, I didn't open it to check, and only found out when I got home that they had given me the wrong order. Another time, I had already paid, giving them two $1 bills and one $5 bill. When I went to pay the remaining balance, the woman at the counter said I had never given her a $2 bill, so I ended up paying an extra $2. I don't usually write restaurant reviews, but I want everyone to be very careful when ordering takeout from their place because the cashiers are dishonest. They only accept cash and don't give reciprocal payments. So I hope everyone will ask about the price before ordering takeout there. This will prevent you from being overcharged. I'm also Chinese, and even though I speak Chinese, I feel they cater more to Fuzhou locals. If you're not from Fuzhou, they might try to take advantage of you. However, the food they make is quite delicious, and the portions are generous. It's hard to find another restaurant that serves such good traditional Fuzhou food.

Also, when I picked up the delivery before, I tried to open it to check if it was the correct order, and the woman at the counter was whispering and giving me unfriendly looks. Another time, I had already paid, giving them two $1 bills and one $5 bill. When I went to pay the remaining balance, the woman at the counter said I had never given her a $2 bill, so I ended up paying an extra $2.

I don't usually write restaurant reviews, but I want everyone to be very careful when ordering takeout from their place because the cashiers are dishonest.

We've had enough hot weather this summer, so walking into a restaurant with little to no air conditioning was honestly uncomfortable. We actually debated leaving before we even ordered, but decided to stick it out. Unfortunately... it never got better. The service also wasn't what I remembered. When you've loved a place for years, you naturally compare it to what you know it can be. I genuinely hope this was just an off night because I have so many great memories here, and I'd honestly love to come back one day and have the Sweet Chick experience that made me fall in love with it in the first place. Because this restaurant has meant a lot to me over the years, and I'm rooting for it. I really am.

review_text_raw:
This one honestly hurt my heart…

Y’all… this review hurts my heart to write because I am a Sweet Chick fan.

Not a “I tried it once” fan. A real fan.

I’ve been going to Sweet Chick since there was only one location in Brooklyn. I was literally traveling from Jersey to Brooklyn just for the food, the drinks, and the experience, and I never minded doing it because it was always worth it.

So when they opened the Ludlow Street location, I was excited because now I didn’t have to make the trip to Brooklyn every time I wanted my chicken and waffles.

Back then, Sweet Chick was an experience.

They had the big specials board with rotating waffles, desserts, and seasonal items. Their chicken and waffles never missed. I honestly can’t remember ever leaving disappointed.

So this review is really hard for me.

Back on June 26th, after work, my mom and I decided to grab dinner. I work in the LES, and she suggested Sweet Chick. I did tell her my brother Robert had gone recently and said it had changed a lot, but we figured we’d see for ourselves.

We got there around 9-ish.

The first thing we noticed…

It was HOT.

Not warm.

Hot.

Like, “why does it feel like a sauna in here?” hot.

We’ve had enough hot weather this summer, so walking into a restaurant with little to no air conditioning was honestly uncomfortable. We actually debated leaving before we even ordered, but decided to stick it out.

Unfortunately… it never got better.

The service also wasn’t what I remembered.

I’m really big on customer service, and Sweet Chick has always had amazing service whenever I’ve gone. This time it just felt different. The attentiveness wasn’t there, and the overall vibe just felt… off.

Even the menu has changed.

My mom used to love their kale salad, but now it’s made differently with things like dates, and she wasn’t interested in it anymore.

For drinks, my mom ordered an espresso martini, and unfortunately she really didn’t enjoy it. It was pretty bitter, and we couldn’t quite figure out what was off about it. If I’m ordering an espresso martini, I have certain expectations, and this one just didn’t hit for her.

I ordered the Queen of New York, and I actually really enjoyed my drink. No complaints there.

Now… the food.

I ordered the Maple Chipotle Chicken & Sweet Potato Waffle.

And this is where my heart really broke.

Years ago, when they first introduced the sweet potato waffle as a special, I remember it actually tasting like sweet potato.

This one…

Honestly just tasted like a regular waffle.

I kept looking for that sweet potato flavor, and it just wasn’t there.

The chicken itself was crispy and cooked well, but the maple chipotle sauce wasn’t evenly coated. Some bites were really good, while other pieces were dry because they barely had any sauce on them.

Another thing longtime Sweet Chick fans might notice is the butter service.

I remember getting three or four different flavored butters, each in their own little container.

This time we got two flavors together in one cup.

It’s a small thing, but it was one of those details that always made Sweet Chick feel special.

My mom ordered the Carolina BBQ Chicken with the Grilled Corn Waffle.

I’ll be fair—her waffle absolutely tasted like a corn waffle. I tried it, and it was really good.

She enjoyed her meal more than I did, although she also had a few pieces of chicken that weren’t evenly coated with sauce and were a little dry.

Overall, she thought it was okay.

And I think that’s really the word for this visit.

Okay.

Not terrible.

But not the Sweet Chick we remembered.

Maybe that’s why this visit hit me so hard.

When you’ve loved a place for years, you naturally compare it to what you know it can be.

I genuinely hope this was just an off night because I have so many great memories here, and I’d honestly love to come back one day and have the Sweet Chick experience that made me fall in love with it in the first place.

Because this restaurant has meant a lot to me over the years, and I’m rooting for it.

I really am.

We ordered the chicken and waffles, and the chicken was badly over-fried. It was so hard it felt like biting into a brick. Normally, I would have sent it back immediately, but my partner didn't want to complain, and after a long drive we were both exhausted.
The fries we ordered were crispy, but lukewarm.  The grits tasted like we got the bottom of the pan they were dry instead of creamy. I also wish they served real maple syrup instead. The waffles were decent, but overall I've definitely had much better chicken and waffles elsewhere.
I was really looking forward to this meal based on all the hype, so it was a big disappointment.

review_text_clean: I came to Raoul's for a burger and left with a new favorite person in Manhattan. Our waitress Amy is a professional comedian disguised as a waitress, and somehow also a professional waitress. Every order came out right, nothing sat empty, and she checked on us with the kind of instinct usually reserved for golden retrievers and mothers of newborns. Great service is rare. Great service from someone who is funnier than your friends is something i didn't know existed until now. Sorry Jamie and Maddie. As for the food, Raoul's clearly knows it has to keep up with her, and it does. The au poivre burger was so good i briefly considered proposing to it: peppery, rich, cooked exactly right. We split the creme brûlée pancake, which is what would happen if a French pastry chef and a Waffle House employee had a sloppy one night stand. Rich, custardy, and gone way too fast. Go for the burger. Stay for the pancake. But whatever you do, ask for Amy. Five stars, and that's only because the scale stops there. Don't ask for a guinness though or you may get laughed out of town. Cheers.

review_text_clean: I was so excited to finally try this Caribbean restaurant. I heard so many good reviews especially being a native New Yorker and already had explored Miss Lilly's and Jasmines. I went on a solo date around late afternoon early evening 4 ish there was only one table sitting 2 woman in the far left towards the back. After settling in I realized inside had been hotter than outside NO A.C nor NO FANS. (The couple that came towards the end of my departure was waving the menu as a fan) I was approached by the waitress "Cat or Kat" I took a minute to order uncertain of what to get the selection was slim. I realized they no longer have 2 additional desserts and no curry goat. I was told they had a special going on today for a "special" for rum punch flavored fruit punch this was no taste of rum and for 18$ I felt robbed. I settled on the brown stew fish with rice & peas and sweet plantains. I asked for a glass of hot water to rinse my utensils off they were a bit foggy the young lady with a accent brung it to me and I was more surprised that she didn't realize there had a been a dead bug I had told her and she absolutely didn't seem shocked by that, to receive a cup of hot water had taken nearly 10-12 minutes because they had ran out of cups with no FOOT traffic only 2 5-6 groups of people had came in since I had been there for over an hour now how they don't have any cups is beyond me....... Finally receiving my hot water my food was warm now I don't know if the fish came warm or was warm within that time I waited but I highly doubt it. I received a new batch of rice it was hot! "Cat or Kat" didn't seem moved by me telling her about the dead bug in the water she didn't ask me afterwards how my food was until I made what shouldn't have been 3 times a "fuss" nor did the young lady with the accent come back to ask me how things were. No discount for the inconvenience was given. This overall experience lacked entirely! No greeting was given when I left I legitimately felt robbed of my experience. All while tipping her 5$ for poor service for what I felt. I won't be returning and I have also uploaded my experience on TikTok and Instagram.

This restaurant is great if you don't really care for good tasting food and need somewhere to sit for no more than 60 minutes.

The performers are incredibly talented, charismatic, and full of energy. Their connection with the audience is effortless, and that energy spreads throughout the room, creating a genuinely memorable experience. The price is fixed and includes a cocktail, appetizer, main course, and dessert. It is certainly not inexpensive, but in my opinion, it is worth every cent considering the quality of both the food and the entertainment. Overall, this was one of the most memorable evenings I have had in New York. If you enjoy great food, live performances, and unique experiences, I highly recommend adding this place to your list.

review_text_clean: I was so excited to visit this bakery in SoHo because I absolutely love cupcakes. Unfortunately, that excitement disappeared the moment I walked in. There were flies sitting directly on the cupcakes on display. I pointed it out to the employee who was restocking the cupcakes. She told another employee, who looked at me like I was crazy for even bringing it up, then simply walked away. No apology. No concern. No attempt to remove the contaminated cupcakes from the display. Nothing. I was honestly shocked. I wasn't expecting some grand gesture, but I certainly expected someone working around food to care that flies were landing on products they were selling to customers. If that's how casually they handle a food safety concern right in front of customers, I can only imagine what's happening in the kitchen. Flies can carry bacteria and contaminate food, and the fact that neither employee seemed remotely bothered was enough for me. I wanted a cupcake SO BAD, but I walked right out. And I'm glad I did. I wouldn't recommend this place based on my experience. Beautiful cupcakes mean nothing if basic food hygiene isn't taken seriously.

First, I have to mention the staff because everyone was incredibly friendly, welcoming, and went out of their way to make sure we had a great experience. Now let’s talk about the food! Everything was fresh, flavorful, and absolutely delicious. The chicken gyro sandwich was incredible, loaded with juicy chicken, fries, and sauce. Every bite was packed with flavor!

Between the delicious food and amazing hospitality, I think I’ve found my new go-to spot for chicken gyros in NYC. I’ll definitely be back!

review_text_clean: It was a nice find when in China Town late. This review is not of the food as we did not eat. The service is less than what I would expect for a wine bar. When we sat we were told the kitchen was closed, but we were only there for a drink so I said we were just looking to grab a drink. The reply was, "Good, cuz that's all we are offering." I suppose it could have been playful, I'll give them the benefit of the doubt there. They don't serve liquor at all so we ordered some wine and chatted. When we were about ready to go, the staff had changed and there was only one bartender left, who was dressed quite casually for the elevated vibe of the bar and it's patrons. We signaled for the check and he handed us a card reader, sat down and waited for us to pay. Once we paid, he stood up, immediately snatched our glasses (which we were not yet finished with) and walked off. Overall, I would say the price we paid was not worth the experience we had. I'm still giving 4 stars as it seemed clean and had a nice atmosphere, just need a bit more staff training.

review_text_clean: For cocktails, I couldn't resist starting with Oxford Street - Monkey Shoulder gin, Fort Hamilton bourbon, Licor 43, and Madeira. It was smooth, pleasantly viscous, and candy-like. I had two. Lori enjoyed the Elderflower Royale - Cimarron blanco tequila, St-Germain, prosecco, and lemon. It was refreshing, yet the tequila gave it some heft. The Oysters Kilpatrick features grilled oysters topped with a slice of cured guanciale and finished with a rich mignonette made with shallots, brown butter, Worcestershire sauce, and malt vinegar. The cured guanciale delivers savory umami, while the brown butter adds rich, nutty flavors and the mignonette base brings tang and brightness. They're first on the menu and should be first on your list. The Crispy Potato with Peekytoe Crab & Lardo is a perfect balance of rich, savory umami and clean, sweet seafood flavors. Texture-wise, it delivers a loud, shatteringly crispy crunch from the potato base that contrasts with the soft, delicate crab meat. The paper-thin lardo melts instantly from the heat, coating your palate in a velvety, luxurious silkiness that ties the entire bite together. Lord's Scotch Egg transforms the traditional British pub classic of pork, sage, thyme, black pepper, and hard-boiled egg into something entirely different: lamb, Madras curry seasoning, a jammy yolk, and panko instead of regular breadcrumbs. It's served hot instead of cold, over herb crème fraîche with mint and chives instead of with mustard on the side. It's one of the best inventions ever and one of the most popular items at the restaurant. The off-menu Welsh Rarebit Burger at Lord's built a cult reputation for god reason. This is definitely one of the best burgers I've ever had. It's easy to see why. A thick 7-ounce prime beef patty comes off the grill charred outside and medium-rare within. Instead of a slice of cheddar, it's smothered in a silky Welsh rarebit sauce built on mustard, Worcestershire, and brown butter. Sharp raw white onion and a soft, pillowy pretzel bun finish it off. It's rich and heavy, but the onion's crunch and sulfurous bite keep all that indulgence in check. By the way, there are no limits on quantities at brunch. The menu is so unique you have to come back and try more. Thank you for the amazing hospitality it was a wonderful experience.

review_text_clean: Good food and a nice experience overall, although there were a few things that I personally didn't care for. For seating, we were placed in a pretty tight area next to a heating pole and near the register. I believe that is the only 2 seater table in the restaurant. The staff's tablet was positioned low on their workstation, while we were seated next to them so whenever they bent over to use it, we happened to have a pretty direct view of their backside. 😅 It was just an awkward seating arrangement, so I'd probably recommend the counter seating instead if you have the option. The pacing was also on the slower side, with quite a bit of time between each course. Our reservation was at 7:30 PM and we didn't leave until 10 PM, so definitely plan to spend a good amount of time here if you're doing the kaiseki menu. One other thing to note is that I had selected a kaiseki set when booking through OpenTable, but when we arrived, we were told the menu had changed a bit, including the pricing. I completely understand that menus and prices can change with seasonal ingredients and other factors, but I would have appreciated seeing the updated information on OpenTable beforehand. The staff were very friendly and the chefs work hard. The food itself was delicious and authentically Japanese. I enjoyed the flavor combinations and how thoughtfully everything came together. For me, this is more of an occasional luxury than somewhere I'd visit regularly. Two kaiseki sets, two drinks, and an additional à la carte dish came to over $400. I probably won't be returning anytime soon, mainly because of the price and the amount of time involved, but I would still recommend it if you're looking for a special Japanese dining experience and don't mind the price or leisurely pace.

Good food and a nice experience overall, although there were a few things that I personally didn’t care for.

For seating, we were placed in a pretty tight area next to a heating pole and near the register. I believe that is the only 2 seater table in the restaurant. The staff’s tablet was positioned low on their workstation, while we were seated next to them so whenever they bent over to use it, we happened to have a pretty direct view of their backside. 😅 It was just an awkward seating arrangement, so I’d probably recommend the counter seating instead if you have the option.

The pacing was also on the slower side, with quite a bit of time between each course. Our reservation was at 7:30 PM and we didn’t leave until 10 PM, so definitely plan to spend a good amount of time here if you’re doing the kaiseki menu.

One other thing to note is that I had selected a kaiseki set when booking through OpenTable, but when we arrived, we were told the menu had changed a bit, including the pricing. I completely understand that menus and prices can change with seasonal ingredients and other factors, but I would have appreciated seeing the updated information on OpenTable beforehand.

The staff were very friendly and the chefs work hard. The food itself was delicious and authentically Japanese. I enjoyed the flavor combinations and how thoughtfully everything came together. For me, this is more of an occasional luxury than somewhere I’d visit regularly. Two kaiseki sets, two drinks, and an additional à la carte dish came to over $400.

I probably won’t be returning anytime soon, mainly because of the price and the amount of time involved, but I would still recommend it if you’re looking for a special Japanese dining experience and don’t mind the price or leisurely pace.

review_text_clean: I used to frequent The Delancey years ago and always had a great experience. Unfortunately, after attending an event here a few months ago, it's clear that management has taken this place in a very different direction, and not for the better. There are prominent signs stating that a 20% gratuity is automatically included and non-negotiable. I have a real problem with this policy. Gratuity should reflect the quality of service and be left to the customer's discretion, not dictated by management or ownership. I opted to pay cash, as I've done in NYC bars for decades, expecting a straightforward transaction where I could tip the bartender myself based on the service. Instead, management insisted on adding both sales tax and a mandatory 20% gratuity, even on cash payments. The poor bartender then had to count out exact change, right down to nickels and dimes, while trying to serve an already busy bar. It's an absurdly inefficient system that inconveniences customers and employees alike, all because of a policy imposed by ownership. To be absolutely clear, this is not a criticism of the bartender. They were excellent, apologetic, and seemed just as frustrated with the policy as we were. This is entirely a management and ownership decision, and they're the ones who should be held accountable. The irony is that we ended up spending considerably less than we otherwise would have and eventually left for another, more customer-friendly bar. At that establishment, I happily tipped well over 20% because the service warranted it. I'm not opposed to tipping generously. Quite the opposite. I'm opposed to businesses removing the customer's discretion and forcing their own employees to enforce policies that create unnecessary friction with customers. Mandatory gratuities should not become the accepted norm in NYC nightlife. Customers have a choice about where to spend their money, and establishments need to understand that policies like this drive business away. It's disappointing to see a place I once enjoyed lose some of what made it a great NYC bar in the first place. Management should seriously reconsider this approach.

review_text_clean: GENDER POLICE!!! writing this weeks later because it doesn't sit right with me still. i had loved this bar despite the odd bathroom policing situation. my friends and i had been here many times before and have been familiar with how seriously they take the whole "bathroom is for customers only" situation. we came in after being out somewhere else before and went right to the bathroom before getting a drink (that we fully intended on buying) and knew the code for the bathroom from the time before. we immediately were followed and told "the bathroom is for customers only" and that we need to buy a drink first. my friend was in the bathroom already at this point and i assured them we will buy a drink and told them the code so they knew i knew it already. as i was telling the security guard this, some woman in plain clothes had walked by and rudely said the same thing. they both had walked away and it was fine until i went into the bathroom and went to close the door but was met with the very same woman STOPPING ME from closing the door with her body and pointing at the sign that it was the "women's bathroom". i was forced out of the bathroom and escorted by the security guard to the one directly next door. MIND YOU both of these restrooms quite literally only have a toilet and a sink in them and i had no clue that they were even "gendered" because i knew they were single stalls. after feeling very uncomfortable from this situation, my friend and i decided to still buy a drink as we were supposed to according to their policy. while we were ordering a drink we saw the very same woman enter the "men's bathroom" and close the door. i decided then a few minutes later to inquire about who this woman was with the bartender where then i was told she does in fact work there with no further details except for the fact that she then was buying me a shot???? at this point i was so confused. I come to find out that the woman in question is the owner who then a few minutes later passed me and my friend an additional free drink like she was doing us a favor but had nothing to say and no apology. to me all of this seemed like she was doing this simply to cover her ass from me saying anything or making a stink. all of this to say, i don't know if i will be returning to an establishment that so heavily polices who uses the bathroom and WHICH bathroom for that matter. as a queer person, i would not recommend this bar.

review_text_clean: Visited on September 8th Casino is a beautifully sexy and elegant restaurant, perfectly situated in a pocket of the Lower East Side where time feels delightfully suspended. It sits in one of the few corners of Manhattan that hasn't been homogenized by rapid gentrification. Here, the true spirit of New York's melting pot remains entirely intact. Looking out, you witness a vibrant crossroads of cultures--a rich diversity that is beautifully mirrored in both the neighborhood's people and the exceptional variety of its culinary landscape. This was my second visit to Casino, and I was eager to return after being blown away by the food, service, and decor the first time. On this second visit, it felt like walking into an entirely different world--in the best way possible. The dining room transported us straight into a 1940s movie, offering a smoky, sexy, and elegant ambiance (minus the actual smoke). My husband and I were celebrating our wedding anniversary, and the team perfectly set the mood by accommodating our request for a red banquette. Our waitress was incredibly warm, friendly, and offered excellent recommendations. When I asked for wine pairings, she seamlessly transitioned us to Daniel, the sommelier. His recommendations were absolutely beautiful, pairing flawlessly with both my appetizer and entree. My only slight disappointment was that he sent our waitress over to pour and sample the wine rather than presenting it himself. He did drop by at the end of our meal but it was bittersweet. My husband and I had a mixed culinary experience here, marked by some disappointing appetizers but truly exceptional pasta dishes. The Grilled Prawns with Calabrian Chili: We were both pretty underwhelmed by this dish. It lacked the vibrant punch we were expecting. The Funghi Fritti (Tempura Battered Mushrooms): Honestly, these were awful. They were literally rock-hard, and no amount of lemon aioli or Calabrian chili sauce was going to rehydrate them. The Main Courses: Bucatini with Clams: My husband opted for this and thought it was delicious. The sauce was absolutely gorgeous; his only minor critique was that he wished there had been a bit more of it. I ordered the Tagliatelle Bolognese: This was the absolute star of the night. It was, without a doubt, the best Bolognese I have ever had in my life. We highly recommend this hidden gem! P.S. The hostess checked on every table except ours.

review_text_clean: The food was solid overall, with a few highlights. We had the pork soup dumplings, green beans, Dan Dan noodles, and ribeye with pepper sauce. The dumpling filling was tender but a little underseasoned, although the vinegar was excellent. At $3 each, they felt a bit overpriced. The Dan Dan noodles were decent but forgettable, while the green beans were delicious and perfectly cooked. The ribeye was very tender and flavorful, served with grilled onions, peppers, and baby corn, but at $60 it didn't feel like a particularly good value. The standout of the meal was actually the ice cream served with the donuts-it was outstanding, both in flavor and texture, and may have been some of the best ice cream I've ever had. The red bean chocolate cake was fine, but we struggled to taste much red bean. The biggest issue was the service and overall atmosphere. The restaurant has 90-minute reservations, which isn't unusual, but here it felt like we were on a countdown from the moment we sat down. Our server approached us almost immediately, staff repeatedly tried to clear plates that still had food on them, and about five seconds after we signed the check, the host asked us to "take our conversation elsewhere" because the next reservation was waiting. He did offer us a spot at the bar, which was appreciated, but the interaction left a poor impression.
