review_text_clean: It's probably because I'm French (the country of origin of the crêpe, born in Brittany) that reading the reviews, almost all of them rave about this establishment, surprises me somewhat... So yes, if we're judging by the quantity served, I can give it 5 stars because one portion is more than enough for two people, but otherwise it's a caloric abomination: My colleague ordered one for $17, and just watching her eat it made me gain weight because it was piled high with brownies, bananas, whipped cream, chocolate, vanilla ice cream, topped with a second layer of chocolate and sprinkled with powdered sugar. All of this was served in an aluminum tray and a to-go bag since there's no seating and the crêperie only has a few tables where you have to eat standing up. In short, an indigestible and unappetizing presentation, at a price where at home you could have a much more balanced, complete meal, served at the table, nicely presented, in a "real" creperie... So not a big fan of this XXL format made in NYC, but there has to be something for everyone and tourists have to adapt to the local cuisine after all!

So yes, if we're judging by the quantity served, I can give it 5 stars because one portion is more than enough for two people, but otherwise it's a caloric abomination:

My colleague ordered one for $17, and just watching her eat it made me gain weight because it was piled high with brownies, bananas, whipped cream, chocolate, vanilla ice cream, topped with a second layer of chocolate and sprinkled with powdered sugar. All of this was served in an aluminum tray and a to-go bag since there's no seating and the crêperie only has a few tables where you have to eat standing up.

In short, an indigestible and unappetizing presentation, at a price where at home you could have a much more balanced, complete meal, served at the table, nicely presented, in a "real" creperie... So not a big fan of this XXL format made in NYC, but there has to be something for everyone and tourists have to adapt to the local cuisine after all!

review_text_clean: I attended an event here tonight and was accused of stealing FREE merchandise. When I walked in, a friendly staff member at the name tag table encouraged me and other attendees to check out the stickers at the table perpendicular to hers. I watched several people ahead of me take merchandise from that table, and when it was my turn, I did the same. I want to emphasize this was FREE merchandise - just like the food and matcha drinks being handed out elsewhere at the event, which nobody else was questioned about. As I zipped up my bag, a staff member approached me and said, "I was not allowed to put that in my bag." I was confused and asked, "You mean the FREE gear we were just told we could take?" He replied, "I have to go check in to see if YOU can have that." I was understandably offended. I had just watched other people take the same items, and I'd been explicitly told it was for everyone. I waited while he went to "verify" something that had already been made clear. He came back and confirmed, with total confidence, what I already knew. What made it worse: I recognized this same staff member from earlier, stationed by the door. When another guest in line asked him why there were two lines, he said he didn't know and pointed down the block to someone else as the "point person." Being singled out and accused like this put a real damper on an event I'd been looking forward to. I'm not writing this review because I was mistaken for a moment - I'm writing it because instead of a simple apology, he doubled down and made me feel like I was in the wrong. In hindsight, I should've escalated it on the spot, but the staff already looked overwhelmed managing the line, and I didn't want to make a scene over stickers. I enjoyed the rest of the event and didn't let his weaponized incompetence ruin my night. But I won't be back , my loss, I guess.

I attended an event here tonight and was accused of stealing FREE merchandise.
When I walked in, a friendly staff member at the name tag table encouraged me and other attendees to check out the stickers at the table perpendicular to hers. I watched several people ahead of me take merchandise from that table, and when it was my turn, I did the same. I want to emphasize this was FREE merchandise — just like the food and matcha drinks being handed out elsewhere at the event, which nobody else was questioned about.
As I zipped up my bag, a staff member approached me and said, "I was not allowed to put that in my bag." I was confused and asked, "You mean the FREE gear we were just told we could take?" He replied, "I have to go check in to see if YOU can have that."
I was understandably offended. I had just watched other people take the same items, and I'd been explicitly told it was for everyone. I waited while he went to "verify" something that had already been made clear. He came back and confirmed, with total confidence, what I already knew.
What made it worse: I recognized this same staff member from earlier, stationed by the door. When another guest in line asked him why there were two lines, he said he didn't know and pointed down the block to someone else as the "point person."
Being singled out and accused like this put a real damper on an event I'd been looking forward to. I'm not writing this review because I was mistaken for a moment — I'm writing it because instead of a simple apology, he doubled down and made me feel like I was in the wrong. In hindsight, I should've escalated it on the spot, but the staff already looked overwhelmed managing the line, and I didn't want to make a scene over stickers.
I enjoyed the rest of the event and didn't let his weaponized incompetence ruin my night. But I won't be back ,  my loss, I guess.

review_text_clean: If you're looking for a satisfying omakase nigiri experience, I would avoid this place if possible. The ambiance was pleasant, and the service was friendly, but unfortunately the food fell well below expectations given $300 per person. We sat at the counter, where there were about five parties ordering omakase but only one head chef preparing everything. He seemed overwhelmed, rushing to make nigiri for the entire counter, and it clearly showed in the quality. I've been to many omakase restaurants throughout New York, and this was easily one of the most disappointing experiences I've had. I asked the chef to substitute the higher mercury fish with something else, and he served gohada instead. I normally enjoy fresh gohada, but this was by far the fishiest one I've ever had. It was so unpleasant that I could barely eat it. Even the otsumami courses were below average, so I don't think there's any justification for ordering the chef's special omakase. For around $80 per person, you can find significantly better omakase in the East Village or Uptown, with much higher quality fish and a far more enjoyable experience.

Bread itself was visually pretty and tasted fine. Not quite feeling like a sourdough, due to somewhat dense and chewy texture but the rye flavor was round and pleasant without being excessive. The slices of toasts are disasters. Look pretty but the toppings are not really making anyone feel like having $60 a loaf special baked good. So mundane and lacking character, and even covering the gentle flavors of the bread entirely. They are pretty to eyes but nothing impressive in flavor. Worst of all, the most expensive menu 'Roe on RYE' -$14 a slice - has salmon roes cover the slice very pretty, but very fishy. 2 of us had some stomach problems on that evening after sharing it. I really love Ikura on any sushi counter, but this was so far from fresh and one of the worst quality salmon roe I had in years. So bad. The staffs are very friendly and nice, but then, it started feeling like mismatch that such nice and elaborate explanations are for such disappointing products. No way to revisit, and would never recommend.

review_text_clean: I have always judged falafel against my great-aunt Victoria's version. I first tasted hers as a preteen, when she stayed with us for several days. She spoke only Arabic and understood a little Spanish, thanks in part to the telenovelas she loved watching. Somehow, we managed to communicate just fine. She cooked up a storm of Lebanese food that week. It was heaven. But she also ruined falafel for me for more than three decades. Try as I might, I could never find a comparable version. They all fell short. By a mile. Until one crisp, picture-perfect autumn day in New York's NoHo neighborhood. I was shopping in the nearby East Village when I asked the store clerk for lunch recommendations. She rattled off a couple of options, but I stopped listening after she mentioned a place serving Arabic food. A few decades on, I was still on the quest for the falafel against which all others were measured. Naturally, it was on the menu. A steal at $13. It's street food, cheap to make and never something you should pay a fortune for. I am eternally hopeful, but when it comes to falafel, my optimism doesn't exactly spring eternal. The cashier was friendly. I would later learn he was the owner's nephew. In the kitchen stood a man and a woman, both short in stature and of undetermined origin. I remember little else, because the moment I took my first bite, I heard the angel chorus. While no two dishes can ever be exactly alike, nothing has come closer to Victoria's falafel than the one at Shifka. Trust me, I've left quite the wake of half-eaten falafel in my life. I told everyone in the shop as much that day and nearly leapt over the counter to kiss the cooks. I will never not visit now whenever I'm in New York. Heck, I may start staying in the neighborhood for easier access. 10/10! Two thumbs up! Five stars! Shifka has restored my faith in falafel. Victoria would be proud, and undoubtedly approve. Alas, my quest has ended!

While my group walked from the bar down to the basement dance floor, I sent a text and put my phone in my front jeans pocket. About 30 seconds later, it was gone. I noticed right away and retraced my steps, but the phone was nowhere to be found. Instead, I ran into six other people frantically searching for their own missing phones and wallets. I asked the bartender several times whether anything had been turned in. He was dismissive and handed me a pre-printed lost items form. The fact that they keep these forms on hand made me think this happens a lot. Then a friend texted me to come upstairs. They had seen the bouncers huddled around my phone, trying to unlock it. Not realizing they were staff, my friend grabbed it. The bouncers became defensive and aggressive toward my friend and were reluctant to hand it over to anyone, including ME. I'm convinced that if my friend hadn't stepped in, I never would have seen my phone again. Based on what I saw, I strongly suspect staff are involved in the thefts here. Do not go unless you want to lose your personal belongings.

review_text_clean: The wine list here is excellent but the real star is the food, which is bold and generous and robustly seasoned but still in harmony with the wine, with all sorts of refined, thoughtful touches that take it beyond the usual cliches of wine bar food into far more exciting culinary territory. We had the charred romano beans, the jimmy nardellos, the tuna tartare with crispy rice pearls, the crab bucatini, the chicken with chermoula, the wagyu picanha, and the pork chop, and they were all fantastic. There's a real authority to the cooking here - it deserves far more recognition than it's currently getting. UPDATE July 2026: Came back again last night and the food is even better than it was the first time. The whole fish is insanely good, as are the lamb chops. There's such generosity, refinement, and flavor in the cooking here, it blows my mind the chef is not getting more recognition. The server said the restaurant will be closing soon, which seems bizarre given how popular the place is and how good the food is. I hope I'm able to eat this chef's food again soon - they are a genius!

review_text_clean: A small downtown wine bar with quite enjoyable food. The wine list was decent with reasonable price, and the food was delicious, especially their pasta. Crab bucatini with smoked trout roe was really good, roasted garlic rigatoni had a predictable but good flavor with generous use of Parmesan. Gem lettuce Caesar salad was a bit disappointing- nothing wrong but quite average with only a few lettuce leaves. Hamachi crudo with cucumber and yuzu was refreshing and well balanced in acidity, yet the fish could have been a little firmer in texture- felt a bit mush. Interior decor appears outdated. Wood burl veneer and square mirror wall panels looked tired and didn't quite deliver neither a sense of classic nor a contemporary. The noise level is problematic. Even understanding it's a wine bar, it was really loud and people were shouting to converse. Low ceiling and hard surface furniture seemed bouncing the sounds a lot.

review_text_clean: So where do I begin. The classic "we'll seat you once your full party arrives." Fair enough. We wait, only to watch another incomplete party get seated ahead of us. Naturally, we ask why. "Oh, because they said the rest of their party is right around the corner." ...Which is exactly what we said. But okay, we move on. We finally sit down and are greeted with the wine and drinks menu. Lovely. Except it takes another 30 minutes for the actual food menu to make an appearance. When we finally order, we ask our waiter what he'd recommend. His response? "I tend to order steak at a steakhouse..." ...is romy a steakhouse? He then proceeds to tell us that the amount of food we've ordered is laughably small. So, against our better judgment, we add a steak. The food arrives at a glacial pace, and by the time we're finished, we're painfully full. Everything is incredibly rich and creamy, and we're left wondering why we were so persuaded to order more food in the first place. The restaurant itself is beautiful. I just wish the experience had lived up to the setting.
